capture.final_message:
Use prime-factor decomposition as the common mechanism.

- For the first statement, write each divisor \(d\mid n\) uniquely as
  \[
  d=\prod_{p\mid n}p^{k_p},\qquad 0\le k_p\le v_p(n).
  \]
  Summing over these independent exponent choices converts the divisor sum into
  \[
  \sum_{d\mid n}d
  =\prod_{p\mid n}\sum_{k=0}^{v_p(n)}p^k.
  \]
  The assumption \(n\ne0\) is essential for the usual finite prime-factorization description of `Nat.divisors`.

- For the second statement, unfold arithmetic-function multiplication as Dirichlet convolution:
  \[
  (f*g)(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}f(d)g(n/d).
  \]
  Since \(n\) is squarefree, every divisor corresponds to choosing a subset of the prime factors of \(n\). Multiplicativity of \(f\) and \(g\) then makes each prime contribute independently: placing \(p\) in \(d\) contributes \(f(p)\), while placing it in \(n/d\) contributes \(g(p)\). Expanding over all choices gives
  \[
  (f*g)(n)=\prod_{p\mid n}\bigl(f(p)+g(p)\bigr),
  \]
  which is exactly the value of `ArithmeticFunction.prodPrimeFactors` in the statement.

The useful intermediate goals are therefore the divisor/exponent parametrization for nonzero \(n\), and the subset-of-prime-factors parametrization for squarefree \(n\). Squarefreeness is crucial in the second identity: higher prime powers would require the full local convolution sum \(\sum_{i=0}^a f(p^i)g(p^{a-i})\), not merely \(f(p)+g(p)\).
